title: The Rocky Mountains, Lander's Peak
why: Bierstadt's mountains are bigger than anything you have ever seen, and the light is just breaking over them.

title: Fur Traders Descending the Missouri
why: Bingham's fur traders drift downriver through pink morning haze, with a cat in the bow and nowhere to hurry to.

title: At the Seaside
why: Chase painted a bright day at the beach with red umbrellas and children digging in the sand.

title: Heart of the Andes
why: Church packed a whole continent into one view, from the snow on the peak to the moss on the rocks at your feet.

title: View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm—The Oxbow
why: Cole's Oxbow is a storm leaving on one side and sun arriving on the other, with the painter alone in between.

title: Watson and the Shark
why: Copley's rescue is one second from going wrong, and nine people are reaching at once.

title: The Chess Players
why: Eakins painted his father watching two old friends play chess in a dark, comfortable room.

title: The Champion Single Sculls (Max Schmitt in a Single Scull)
why: Eakins put his friend alone on a glassy river in clear autumn light, resting between strokes.

title: Approaching Thunder Storm
why: Heade painted the minute before a storm: black sky, flat water, and one man on the shore who has not moved yet.

title: The Gulf Stream
why: Homer's sailor is adrift with sharks circling and a waterspout coming, and he is not looking at either.

title: The Veteran in a New Field
why: Homer's veteran has put down his rifle and picked up a scythe. Hot sun, tall wheat, and a lot to think about.

title: Lake George
why: Kensett's Lake George is a still morning with nothing moving. The quietest picture in the wing.

title: Washington Crossing the Delaware
why: Leutze's boat is overloaded, the river is full of ice, and every person in it is pulling in the same direction.

title: Madame X (Virginie Amélie Avegno Gautreau)
why: Sargent's Madame X turns her face away and lets you look. Composed on the outside, and a scandal underneath.

title: George Washington
why: Stuart left this portrait of Washington unfinished on purpose, and kept it to copy for the rest of his life.

title: Armor (Yoroi) of Ashikaga Takauji (1305–1358)
medium: Iron, lacquer, leather, silk, gilt copper
why: A fourteenth-century samurai armor of silk cord and lacquered scales, made for a man who founded a dynasty.

title: Armor (Gusoku)
why: Dark lacquer, blue silk and a quiet, upright posture. This armor is about discipline, not display.

title: Burgonet
why: Negroli hammered a mermaid and a Medusa out of one sheet of steel. Close up, the detail stops time.

title: Sallet in the Shape of a Lion's Head
medium: Steel, copper, gold, glass, pigment, textile
why: A helmet shaped like a roaring gilt lion. Somebody wanted to be noticed, and five hundred years later they still are.

title: Helm for the Joust of Peace (Stechhelm)
why: A frog-mouth helm for the joust, built for the roar of a crowd and the moment two riders meet.

title: Horse Armor Made for Johann Ernst, Duke of Saxony-Coburg (1521–1553)
why: Lochner made this horse armor for a duke who liked to be looked at. The whole court rides in a line.

title:
Armor Garniture of George Clifford (1558–1605), 
Third Earl of Cumberland
why: George Clifford had this blued and gilded armor made for tilting in front of the Queen. Confidence in steel.

title: Armor of Emperor Ferdinand I (1503–1564)
why: Ferdinand I rode into the Equestrian Court in this. It still has the feel of a parade.

title: Armor of Henry II, King of France (reigned 1547–59)
why: Henry II's parade armor is covered in gold and silver figures. It was never meant for a fight, only for being seen.

title: Shield
medium: Wood, linen, gesso, gold leaf, polychromy
why: Girolamo da Treviso painted a whole battle onto a parade shield, gold on dark ground, horses everywhere.

title: Costume Armor in the Classical Style
medium: Helmet: linen, papier-mâché, bole, gold leaf, graphite; tunic: silk, cotton, metal coils and spangles, metallic yarn
why: Fancy-dress armor for a costume ball in 1790, made to look like a Roman hero. Pure theater.

title: Armor of Infante Luis, Prince of Asturias (1707–1724)
medium: Steel, gold, brass, silk, cotton, metallic yarn, paper
why: A tiny gilded armor made for a five-year-old prince. Equal parts serious and sweet.

title: Harquebusier's Armor of Pedro II, King of Portugal (reigned 1683–1706) with Buff Coat
date: ca. 1683 and later; buff coat, 17th–18th century
why: Black steel and gilt for a king of Portugal. Armor from the last century anyone wore it to war.

title: Ema (Votive Painting) of a Chinese Lion and Peony Tree
medium: Ink, color, and gold leaf on wood
why: A huge votive painting of a lion tumbling through peonies, made to hang in a shrine and be seen from far away.

title: Avalokiteshvara, the Bodhisattva of Infinite Compassion
why: Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, carved by the Tenth Karmapa with a soft, almost shy face.

title: Shiva as Lord of Dance (Nataraja)
why: Shiva dances inside a ring of fire, one foot raised, perfectly balanced in the middle of everything ending and starting again.

title: Wooded Mountains at Dusk
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on paper
why: Kuncan painted dense wooded mountains at dusk with a poem about hiding out from the world. A picture for going inside.

title: Jar with dragon
medium: Porcelain painted with cobalt blue under transparent glaze (Jingdezhen ware)
why: A blue-and-white jar with a dragon wrapped all the way around it, mid-flight and grinning.

title: The Sound of Spring in a Lonely Valley
why: Hongren, a monk-painter, drew a valley with almost nothing in it. The title says you can hear spring arriving.

title: Boulder with Daoist paradise
why: A jade boulder carved into a Daoist paradise: pines, pavilions and tiny immortals climbing toward the top.

title: Horse and female rider
why: A Tang dynasty woman on horseback, sitting easy, ready to ride out. Thirteen hundred years old and still going somewhere.

title: Buddha of Medicine Bhaishajyaguru (Yaoshi fo)
medium: Water-based pigment over foundation of clay mixed with straw
why: A whole temple wall of the Medicine Buddha, fifty feet wide, surrounded by attendants. Walk up close and it holds still for you.

title: Landscape in Moonlight
medium: One of a triptych of hanging scrolls; ink on silk
why: Kano Tanyu's landscape in moonlight is mostly mist and silver. A screen for a quiet evening.

title: Orchid and rock
why: Ma Shouzhen painted one orchid and one rock in a few quick strokes. Nothing wasted, nothing missing.

title: Wintry mountains
why: Gong Xian built these wintry mountains out of thousands of small dark dots. Bleak, patient, and strangely comforting.

title: Scenes of the Four Seasons in Kyoto
medium: Handscroll; ink and color on silk
why: Genki painted a year in Kyoto, with hundreds of small people out walking in every season. You are one of them.

title: Cubiculum (bedroom) from the Villa of P. Fannius Synistor at Boscoreale
why: A whole Roman bedroom from a villa buried by Vesuvius, painted red and gold. Step inside and close the door on the day.

title: Bronze statue of the emperor Trebonianus Gallus
why: An eight-foot bronze of the emperor Trebonianus Gallus, one of very few to survive. Heavy, odd and impossible to ignore.

title: Bronze diskos thrower
why: A small bronze diskos thrower caught at the top of the wind-up. All of the energy is still to come.

title: Marble portrait of the emperor Augustus
why: Augustus, carved to look calm and ageless. A face made to say that everything is under control.

title: Marble statue of an old woman
why: A Roman marble of an old market woman on her way to a festival, basket in hand, tired and determined.

title: Marble statue of a lion
why: A marble lion that once guarded a tomb, mouth open, still keeping watch.

title: Marble grave stele with a family group
why: A family group on a grave marker, clasping hands. People holding on to each other, carved in marble.

title: Terracotta neck-amphora (jar) with lid and knob (27.16)
why: An amphora by Exekias, the finest of the black-figure painters. Small figures doing precise things, beautifully.

title: Wall painting: Perseus and Andromeda in landscape, from the imperial villa at Boscotrecase
date: last decade of the 1st century BCE
why: Perseus swooping in to rescue Andromeda, painted on a Roman wall in a landscape full of air and distance.

title: Marble grave stele of a little girl
why: The grave stele of a little girl holding her two pet doves. Quiet, tender and very old.

title: Marble statue of a kouros (youth)
why: The kouros has stood with one foot forward and a small smile for 2,600 years. Young, upright, and about to walk.

title: Marble portrait of the emperor Caracalla
why: Caracalla scowling over his shoulder. The most honest portrait of a bad mood in the building.

title: Bronze statue of Eros sleeping
why: Eros, the god of love, fast asleep on a rock with his wings folded. Permission to rest.

title: Marble seated harp player
why: A marble harp player, head tipped back, lost in a tune from nearly five thousand years ago.

title: Marble sarcophagus with the Triumph of Dionysos and the Seasons
why: A sarcophagus crowded with Dionysos, panthers, satyrs and the four seasons. A party carved in stone.

title: Marble Statue Group of the Three Graces
why: The Three Graces with their arms around each other. Friendship, in marble, for two thousand years.

title: The Horse Fair
why: Rosa Bonheur's Horse Fair is sixteen feet of muscle, dust and shouting. It is impossible to stand still in front of it.

title: The Harvesters
why: Bruegel's harvesters eat, nap and work under a hazy late-summer sky, and nobody is in a rush.

title: Piazza San Marco
why: Canaletto's Piazza San Marco is full of people going somewhere, under a sky that has just cleared.

title: The Musicians
why: Caravaggio crowded four young musicians into one warm room, half tuning up and half daydreaming.

title: The Card Players
why: Cezanne's card players have said everything they need to say. Two people, one table, total concentration.

title: Soap Bubbles
why: Chardin's boy is giving all of his attention to one soap bubble, and for a moment so are you.

title: Hagar in the Wilderness
why: Corot's Hagar is at the end of her strength in an empty landscape, and help is just arriving.

title: The Third-Class Carriage
why: Daumier's third-class carriage is tired strangers pressed together, each lost in their own thoughts.

title: The Rest on the Flight into Egypt
why: Gerard David's holy family stops to rest on a long journey. The grass is soft and the day is kind.

title: The Death of Socrates
why: David's Socrates keeps talking, calm and certain, while the people who love him fall apart around him.

title: The Crucifixion; The Last Judgment
medium: Oil on canvas, transferred from wood
why: Van Eyck fit a whole crowded world into two small panels, every face and cloud painted as if it mattered.

title: Irises
why: Van Gogh's irises push up against a yellow wall, every one of them a little different and all of them alive.

title: Self-Portrait with a Straw Hat (obverse: The Potato Peeler)
why: Van Gogh painted himself in a straw hat because he could not afford a model, in quick, nervous strokes of yellow.

title: Roses
why: Van Gogh painted these roses in his last spring, in the week he left the asylum, and they are pure relief.

title: Wheat Field with Cypresses
why: Van Gogh painted a restless, swirling sky over a calm golden field.

title: Manuel Osorio Manrique de Zuñiga (1784–1792)
why: Goya's little boy in red stands very still while the cats watch his pet magpie. Tender, and a bit uneasy.

title: The Penitent Magdalen
why: La Tour's Magdalen sits alone with a single candle, letting a hard thought settle.

title: Boating
why: Manet's Boating is a bright afternoon on the water with someone you like and nowhere to be.

title: Haystacks: Autumn
why: Millet's haystacks sit in the last warm light of autumn, with the shepherd and his flock already heading home.

title: The Abduction of the Sabine Women
why: Poussin's Sabine Women is all motion and noise, every figure pulling in a different direction.

title: Aristotle with a Bust of Homer
why: Rembrandt's Aristotle rests a hand on Homer's head and thinks about what lasts, in gold light and deep shadow.

title: Self-Portrait
why: Rembrandt at fifty-four, looking at himself without flattery and without flinching.

title: By the Seashore
why: Renoir sat a friend in a wicker chair by the sea and let the whole afternoon go soft around her.

title: Wheat Fields
why: Ruisdael gives you a wide road, ripe wheat and a sky that takes up most of the picture.

title: Circus Sideshow (Parade de cirque)
why: Seurat's sideshow is a crowd at night, lit by gas lamps, waiting to be let in. Quiet, strange, together.

title: The Englishman (William Tom Warrener, 1861–1934) at the Moulin Rouge
why: Toulouse-Lautrec caught an Englishman at the Moulin Rouge mid-flirt, in a room that is all noise and color.

title: Whalers
why: Turner's whalers are barely there, swallowed by spray and weather. A storm you can feel in your chest.

title: Juan de Pareja (ca. 1608–1670)
artist: Velázquez (Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez)
why: Velazquez painted his assistant Juan de Pareja looking straight back at you with quiet, unshakable dignity.

title: Young Woman with a Water Pitcher
why: Vermeer caught a woman alone at a window in the first soft light of the day, and nothing else needs to happen.

title: Mezzetin
why: Watteau's Mezzetin plays his guitar to someone who has already turned away. Sweet, sad and a little funny.

title: Two Men Contemplating the Moon
why: Friedrich's two friends stand in the dark and look at the moon together, saying nothing.

title: The Abduction of Rebecca
why: Delacroix painted a rescue in the middle of a burning castle, all hot color and panic.

title: Madame Georges Charpentier (Marguerite-Louise Lemonnier, 1848–1904) and Her Children, Georgette-Berthe (1872–1945) and Paul-Emile-Charles (1875–1895)
why: Renoir painted a mother, two children and a very patient dog in a room that feels like home.

title: The Dance Class
why: Degas caught a dance class between exercises: fidgeting, stretching, whispering, waiting to begin.

title: Ia Orana Maria (Hail Mary)
why: Gauguin moved the Annunciation to Tahiti and filled it with fruit, flowers and heat.

title: Game of Hounds and Jackals
why: A board game from 1800 BCE with ivory hounds and jackals for pieces. Somebody played this with a friend.

title: Mastaba Tomb of Perneb
why: You can walk into Perneb's tomb. Four thousand years old, cool, dim and very still.

title: Gazelle
why: An ivory gazelle, alert and about to move, standing on a little hill of desert flowers.

title: Cat Statuette intended to contain a mummified cat
why: A bronze cat sitting perfectly upright with gold earrings. Composed, a little aloof, and not going anywhere.

title: Senwosret III as a Sphinx
why: Senwosret III has the most tired, thoughtful face in the whole museum. A king who had seen a lot.

title: Travelling Boat being Rowed
medium: Wood, paint, gesso, linen twine and linen fabric
why: A little wooden boat with a whole crew rowing in time. Meketre packed it for the afterlife so he would never travel alone.

title: Hippopotamus ("William")
why: William the hippo is small, blue and covered in lotus flowers. Nobody leaves him without smiling.

title: Stela of the Steward Mentuwoser
why: Mentuwoser sits at a table piled with food while his family brings more. A picture of being looked after.

title: Coffin of Khnumnakht
why: Khnumnakht's coffin is painted with eyes so he could look out, and a door so he could leave. Grief, made practical.

title: Sphinx of Hatshepsut
why: Hatshepsut as a sphinx: a queen who ruled as king, carved in granite and completely sure of herself.

title: Haremhab as a Scribe of the King
why: Haremhab, before he was pharaoh, sitting cross-legged with a scroll and his head down, working.

title: Model of a Granary with Scribes
why: A model granary with tiny scribes counting the grain. Ordinary work, done carefully, made to last forever.

title: The Temple of Dendur
why: The Temple of Dendur sits beside a pool under a wall of glass. Sit on the ledge and let the room go quiet.

title: Portrait of the Boy Eutyches
why: Eutyches was a boy in Roman Egypt. His portrait looks straight at you across two thousand years.

title: Book of the Dead for the Chantress of Amun, Nauny
why: Nauny's Book of the Dead shows her heart being weighed against a feather. A long scroll about facing yourself.

title: Lake Biwa in Four Seasons
medium: Pair of six-panel folding screens; ink and color on paper
why: Lake Biwa in four seasons, painted by a calligrapher. The same water, four different moods.

title: Birds and Flowers
medium: Set of three hanging scrolls; ink and color on paper
why: Kano Motonobu filled a pair of screens with birds, blossom and running water. Spring, at full volume.
